title: No One Perfect As Van Foreest, Martirosyan Hit Back In Total Chess Fast Classic
summary:
GMs Jorden van Foreest and Haik Martirosyan hit back from round-one losses to beat GMs Levon Aronian and Shakhriyar Mamedyarov as the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 Group Stage began. GMs Alireza Firouzja, Fabiano Caruana, Jan-Krzysztof Duda, Liem Le, Ian Nepomniachtchi, and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave all lead their groups on four points after a win and a draw, with the latter two just missing out on second wins. GM Magnus Carlsen was held to two incredibly fighting draws by GM Anish Giri, with both players on 2/6 and with work to do.

Day three, which features rounds three and four of the Group Stage, is on Thursday, November 12, starting at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST.

Group A: Firouzja, Duda Lead, Van Foreest Hits Back Vs. Aronian

Group B: Caruana, Le Lead

Group C: Nepomniachtchi Leads, Martirosyan Hits Back, Carlsen-Giri Make Thrilling Draws

Group D: MVL Misses Perfection, Assaubayeva Holds So To 2 Draws

The all-important Group Stage—only group winners will get a chance to play for the title—features five days of double-rounds of 45-minute "fast classic" chess, where players face the same opponent twice, with reversed colors. The first round saw half the games end decisively.

Group Stage: Round 1

In the second round, just four games were decisive after some very near misses, while Martirosyan and Van Foreest stood out for their comebacks—meaning they'd outscored the players who made two draws on the day, since a win is worth three points and a draw only one.

Group Stage: Round 2

You can check out GM Hikaru Nakamura's recap of the first day of classical action:

Group A: Firouzja, Duda Lead, Van Foreest Hits Back Vs. Aronian

GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov finished in a shocking 22nd place in the blitz tiebreaker, and his fortunes didn't improve as the classical chess began. Firouzja explained his tactics as, "My idea was putting pressure all the time, and at the end I managed to get some tricks."

Abdusattorov's 35...Bf7? lost a pawn by force when Firouzja didn't move his attacked rook, and the French star never relaxed his grip.

Abdusattorov resigns vs. Firouzja. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

That was the last game to finish in the first round, with Firouzja saying of the 45-minute format, "It's still too long!" and lamenting, "To play a second game is very difficult, but it’s life!"

Perhaps exhaustion was a factor as Abdusattorov did come close to hitting back, but the Uzbek star missed a chance to win a pawn as the second game fizzled out into a 57-move draw.

Jorden van Foreest was first into the confessional... and first to lose a game! Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

One player who did manage to hit back, however, was Van Foreest, who had a lively day. He commented, "I thought this is my chance to be the first person," as he visited the confessional, explaining he'd taken a "high risk, high reward" approach to the opening against Aronian. The momentum would soon swing, however, with Aronian himself coming to the confessional.

Levon Aronian: "The good thing is I don't remember anything... and I'm happy!" https://t.co/nT26Udm5Nr https://t.co/nlTBf3ipiL

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 11, 2026

Van Foreest later summed up, "I was also the first to lose, which was interesting!" with Aronian's high spirits justified by what happened on the board. The Dutchman went astray on move 15 and saw his position rapidly collapse.

"I decided to go all-in!" said Van Foreest of his decision to play the King's Indian Defense in game two, and it worked to perfection when Aronian lashed out with 21.f5?!. Aronian called his play "careless," while Van Foreest said, "I got all the squares." He put them to good use to win our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao analyzes below.

Firouzja is joined in the group A lead by Duda, who overcame GM Andrew Hong.

Jan-Krzysztof Duda talking to the Norwegian media. Photo: Total Chess.

The first game ended in a draw after both sides got chances, while in the second Duda "converted" a huge space edge on the board into a 10-minute lead on the clock. That proved decisive as Hong was unable to navigate a difficult position and was gradually outplayed.

Group B: Caruana, Le Lead

The B group also has two leaders, with Caruana getting off to what he called "a perfect start" against GM Richard Rapport, as he took over early and ground out a win with the black pieces. The world number-three could have ended the day on a perfect score, but couldn't convert pressure in the second game into another win.

Peter Leko made the ceremonial opening move for his Hungarian colleague. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Le, meanwhile, made a rock-solid draw against GM Vladislav Artemiev, afterward crediting his friend and former student GM Awonder Liang for playing the same opening as Artemiev in a training game before the event. In the second game, meanwhile, we got the day's craziest time trouble, as Artemiev found himself 40 minutes down on the clock!

Potentially that was survivable, since the 30-second increment still allows players to gain time, but for once Artemiev wasn't able to hold it together. He soon got into trouble and, in an already borderline lost position, allowed the beautiful blow 22.Nd5!!.

Another player to suffer on the clock was GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, who got down to under four minutes on move 15 against GM Vincent Keymer in their first game but still managed to hold a draw. "More than the game, I think my time management was so off," said Praggnanandhaa afterward, and in the second game he also got into trouble on the clock and cracked.

Keymer twice came close to beating Praggnanandhaa. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

That wasn't the end of the story, however, with Keymer saying "everything worked perfectly" until he made one "insane move."

"I just got lucky," said Praggnanandhaa.

Group C: Nepomniachtchi Leads, Martirosyan Hits Back, Carlsen-Giri Make Thrilling Draws

The world number-one's group always gets special attention, but it was Nepomniachtchi who nearly ended the day on a perfect score. Against GM Abhimanyu Mishra, he explained his approach in the first game as, "My plan was to wait until he runs out of time and then just complicate things, and that’s exactly what I did!"

Nepomniachtchi couldn't make it 6/6 against Mishra. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Nepomniachtchi sacrificed two pawns for attacking chances, and 51...b5? was the single mistake that cost Mishra the game.

Both players pointed to the same tactical point in the play that followed.

Mishra was on the ropes in the second game, but Nepomniachtchi missed an endgame win—for once rushing can't be blamed, as he spent four minutes at the key moment—and the game ended in a 98-move draw. It was hard to know who was most upset at the end. Nepomniachtchi had missed a chance, but Mishra commented, "The game is just horrible!" of the torture he'd endured.

The second game was disappointing for both players! Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

The format of facing the same opponent twice can be brutal, but it also gives chances of redemption. Martirosyan made one bad move early on against Mamedyarov in the first game and was then comprehensively outplayed with the black pieces. Just like Van Foreest, however, he managed to hit back, calling it "really special" and noting, "It’s really good that we have so many games in a day, especially after losing."

Martirosyan pulled off a comeback after a tough loss. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Mamedyarov was under early pressure, fell behind on the clock, and, after a blunder on move 20, resigned the next move.

Still, despite that painful reversal, Mamedyarov has more points than two players who "only" drew their games, Giri and Carlsen.

Both clashes were thrillers, with Carlsen opening with the Dutch Defense in the first game and getting the kind of strategically risky position we could expect. Giri's 16.d5!? was an interesting pawn sacrifice (there was nothing wrong with 16.dxc5) that left the game balanced on a knife-edge as both players ran out of time.

In the end, however, Carlsen managed to exchange off queens into the safety of an endgame he could play on the 30-second increment. No one would have been surprised if he'd also gone on to win, but this time there was no endgame magic.

Giri and Carlsen had their first lively post-mortem of the day. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

That was perhaps only a warm-up for the second game, which was wild and featured brilliant play by both players. Carlsen and Giri took turns at looking likely winners, before a peaceful outcome ensued.

And again a huge fight ended amicably. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Both players will have to start scoring more heavily, since only first place in the group gives a chance to play a four-player knockout for the title.

Group D: MVL Misses Perfection, Assaubayeva Holds So To 2 Draws

Curiously, both female players ended up in the same group, and both could be happy with how their day went. GM Bibisara Assaubayeva had suffered in blitz the day before, losing eight games before making a single draw against GM Vaishali Rameshbabu. In classical, however, she made two draws against the world number-six, GM Wesley So, and it could have been better, since she was briefly winning in the first game.

Assaubayeva made an impressive two draws against So. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

So then shut down the second game early for another draw, with the two draws costing six rating points. That meant he was unable to exploit Abdusattorov's loss to climb to world number-five on the live rating list.

Vaishali, meanwhile, had starred in blitz but suffered a tough loss in the first classical game. At the critical moment she could still escape, but it was anything but easy despite the computer 0.00 evaluation.

Vachier-Lagrave had an extra pawn, a better pawn structure, and a huge time advantage in the second game, but he let Vaishali escape and draw via a rook endgame. The Frenchman's speed had let him down, but as GM David Howell commented about this game, "A player’s greatest strength is often their greatest weakness."

Maxime Vachier-Lagrave came close to two wins. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Vachier-Lagrave still has a two-point lead over the next four players in the group, since GMs Arjun Erigaisi and Hans Niemann also made two draws. The first was utterly unremarkable, while the second was wild, with Niemann close to a win that would have taken him back into the 2700 club, before Arjun sacrificed an exchange to get right back into the game and make all three results appear possible.

The queue to get into the Anantara New York Palace venue in Budapest. Photo: Tor Nilssen/Total Chess.

This is just the start, since we have another four days of action, with the stakes gradually growing. The matchups in round three look as follows:

Round 3 Pairings

How to watch?

You can review the event on the Chess24 Twitch or YouTube pages, or on GM Hikaru Nakamura's Kick channel. You can find the games on our dedicated events page.

The live broadcast was hosted by GM David Howell, IMs Jovanka Houska and Anna Rudolf, and WIM Fiona Steil-Antoni.

The Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 takes place on November 10-21 at the Anantara New York Palace Hotel in Budapest, Hungary. The event is a trial run for the official event in 2027, which will crown the first FIDE World Combined Champion. The event consists of a round-robin group stage and a knockout combining blitz, rapid, and fast classical time controls. The time control is 3+2 for blitz, 15+10 for rapid, 45+30 for fast classical, and 10 minutes (White) vs. 7 minutes (Black) with a one-second increment starting on move 41 in armageddon.

title: Chessboxing World Championship Set For Istanbul After '60 Minutes' Spotlight
summary:
Chess continues to grow, and now chessboxing is gaining momentum too. More than 200 fighters from at least 25 countries are expected at the eighth Chessboxing World Championship, Presented by Lords Mobile in Istanbul on November 16-21. The event follows a year of increased attention after CBS' 60 Minutes introduced the sport to 20 million people worldwide.

The championships begin exactly a year after a roughly 13-minute segment aired on November 16, 2025. Introducing the sport, correspondent Bill Whitaker said:

"When we first heard about chess boxing, we thought it was a joke. Chess boxing? Could it really be a thing? Turns out it is, and it's just what it sounds like: alternate rounds of chess and boxing."

Team USA coach Matt Thomas, known as "the voice of chess boxing," says the impact extended well beyond television.

"Our '60 Minutes' segment changed the trajectory for not just the Team USA program, but the growth of the sport worldwide," Thomas told Chess.com.

Our '60 Minutes' segment changed the trajectory for not just the Team USA program, but the growth of the sport worldwide.

—Matt Thomas

He said dozens of people contacted the team wanting to try out the sport after the broadcast, while hundreds reached out about starting or joining a local chessboxing club. That helped the organizers find locations for their first Team USA Tryout Tour.

"Thanks to our sponsor, MoonPay, we were able to visit six cities, set up clubs in each, and recruit top talent to fill our ranks this year," Thomas said.

Matt Thomas is a former Chess Boxing World Champion, streamer and founder of United Chessboxing.

The U.S. team will, however, travel without its reigning super heavyweight champion. FM James Canty III will not defend his title after winning last year's championship in Serbia, Thomas confirmed.

Canty won both of his bouts at the 2025 championship, defeating Kazakhstan's Sayan Shayakhmetov in the semifinals and Russia's Evgenii Isaev in the final. Canty’s success depended on surviving in the ring long enough to make his superior speed on the chessboard count.

Thomas remains confident in the team heading to Istanbul. "Even without our super heavyweight champ returning, we have the most talented Team USA in history with plenty of rising stars to look out for," he said.

Among the fighters Thomas highlighted are:

FM Arslan Otchiyev, a professional mixed martial arts fighter and founder of e4 Chess Academy in Connecticut. Thomas described him as the "new best pound-for-pound chessboxer in the world."

NM Deepak Aaron, a four-time Georgia state chess champion and three-time New York youth state champion, whose grandfather, IM Manuel Aaron, was India's first international master.

FM William Graif, the 2025 New York State blitz champion, who Thomas said earned "Fight of the Tournament" honors at last year's worlds.

Edward Green, a U.S. Marine and returning silver medalist with a professional MMA background.

Heather Brown, a streamer and head of North Brooklyn Chess, whom Thomas identified as Team USA's first female fighter in classic chessboxing.

Returning world champions from the Masters Division include team captain Tuba Bayram, Burak Gezen, and Nick Sonnenberg, looking to defend their titles.

More than 200 fighters from 25 countries will take part in Istanbul. Here's Matt Thomas observing a fight. Photo: Chessboxing.

The U.S. team has launched a fundraiser, and hopes to raise $25,000 for the team's expenses ahead of and during the championship.

France is also bringing a big team of 28 fighters, the largest delegation to date, including four women, Sportmag reports. Among them is three-time World Champion Valentin Marcel, who won titles in 2022, 2023, and 2024. The French federation is helping organize the event along with the Turkish hosts.

The World Chess Boxing Organisation (WCBO) Championships will take place at the Selectum City Atasehir hotel, with strategy game Lords Mobile as the main sponsor.

The athletes will compete for titles across weight divisions in men's, women's, junior, and masters categories. Bouts alternate between three-minute rounds of chess and boxing, with a one-minute break between rounds. Victory can come through checkmate, a knockout or technical knockout, an opponent running out of chess time, or resignation.

Team USA at last year's Chess Boxing World Championship.

The qualification rounds and semifinals use a five-round format: three chess rounds and two boxing rounds, with each player starting with four minutes and 30 seconds on the chess clock. Finals are seven rounds, four chess and three boxing, with six minutes per player. If the chess game is drawn, boxing points decide the winner, with further tiebreak rules if those scores are also level.

Finals are scheduled for November 21, including an evening gala, followed by the closing ceremony late that night.

title: Firouzja, Caruana, Nepomniachtchi and Vachier-Lagrave lead after opening Fast Classic day in Budapest
summary: Ten decisive outcomes mark the start of the Total Chess round-robin group stage The Fast Classic group stage of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot began in Budapest with an action-packed opening day, as 24 of the world’s leading players contested two games each across four groups. Day 1 produced 10 decisive outcomes from 24 games, immediately putting the tournament’s three-points-for-a-win scoring system into focus. Each player faced the same opponent twice, with colours reversed in the second game. After the opening day, Alireza Firouzja and Jan-Krzysztof Duda share the lead on four points in Group A, Fabiano Caruana and Le Quand Liem  are level on top in Group B, while Ian Nepomniachtchi and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave are the outright leaders of Groups C and D respectively. The pre-event Blitz standings are used to separate players tied on points, placing Firouzja and Caruana at the top of their respective groups. Firouzja and Duda set the pace in Group A Alireza Firouzja made a strong start against Nodirbek Abdusattorov, winning his first game after a long battle. Firouzja took full advantage of a critical mistake by his opponent and converted the resulting winning position. Their return encounter was much tighter. Abdusattorov generated chances and at one stage held an advantage, but Firouzja defended well, and the game eventually ended in a draw. The four points leave Firouzja at the top of Group A. Jan-Krzysztof Duda matched Firouzja’s four-point total. After drawing his opening game with Andrew Hong, the Polish grandmaster won the return game with White, gradually taking control before successfully converting his advantage into a win. Levon Aronian and Jorden van Foreest produced the most symmetrical result of the group. Aronian won their first encounter with the black pieces before Van Foreest struck back by winning the return game, also with Black. Both finished the opening day on three points. Caruana and Le share the Group B lead Fabiano Caruana began his Fast Classic campaign with an important victory over local star Richard Rapport. Playing with Black, Caruana emerged on top after a tense struggle. The return game developed differently, with neither player ultimately able to create a decisive breakthrough. The draw took Caruana to four points and, thanks to his higher Blitz ranking, first place in Group B after Day 1. Le Quang Liem  also collected four points from his two games against Vladislav Artemiev. Their first encounter ended in a draw, but Le struck in the return game. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Vincent Keymer could not be separated, drawing both encounters and finishing the day on two points each. Nepomniachtchi leads as Carlsen and Giri draw twice Group C produced one of the most intriguing opening-day stories. World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen and Dutch No. 1 Anish Giri drew both of their games. Their first encounter remained balanced throughout, and the return game followed a similar pattern, with neither player able to tip the balance in their favour. Both therefore finish Day 1 on two points. Ian Nepomniachtchi made the strongest start in the group. He defeated Abhimanyu Mishra in the first game after a long battle before Mishra held the return encounter to a draw. Nepomniachtchi’s four points give him sole possession of the Group C lead. Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and Haik Martirosyan traded blows, both winning with Black. Mamedyarov struck first, before Martirosyan immediately retaliated in the return game after capitalizing on the opponent’s mistake. Both end the day on three points. Vachier-Lagrave emerges as the outright Group D leader Maxime Vachier-Lagrave was the only player in Group D to record a decisive result on the opening day. Facing Vaishali Rameshbabu with Black in their first game, Vachier-Lagrave remained patient in a balanced endgame before a late error by Vaishali allowed him to seize the advantage and convert. Their second game ended in a draw, giving the French grandmaster four points and the outright group lead. All other games in Group D ended in draws. The Fast Classic group stage continues in Budapest with another two games per player on Thursday as the race for the knockout brackets begins to take shape. Text: Total Chess Photos: Total Chess / Maria Emelianova and Michal Walusza Official website: www.totalchess.com About Total Chess Total Chess is a global championship platform established to redefine elite competitive chess for the modern era. Developed by Norway Chess and approved by FIDE, the Total Chess World Championship Tour introduces a unified format that crowns the world’s ultimate champion by testing excellence across three disciplines: Fast Classical, Rapid and Blitz. The Tour will bring together the world’s top 24 men and women players to compete across four premier international events hosted in leading global cities. Designed to elevate the sport’s commercial appeal and fan engagement, Total Chess combines world-class competition with innovation, technology and immersive spectator experiences to create a new benchmark for professional chess. With a vision to make chess one of the world’s most engaging and commercially sustainable sports, Total Chess aims to expand the game’s global footprint, inspire the next generation of players, and connect millions of fans through a dynamic championship that celebrates intelligence, strategy and sporting excellence.

title: FIDE President Timur Turlov holds meetings in Budapest
summary: President of the International Chess Federation Timur Turlov visited Budapest, where he attended the opening ceremony of the Total Chess Pilot 2026 tournament and held a series of meetings. The main focus of the negotiations was on expanding international cooperation and developing new areas of FIDE’s activities. During the visit, Timur Turlov met with the Rector of the Hungarian University of Sports Science, Professor Tamás Sterbenz. The parties discussed prospects for cooperation in the field of sports education, including the possibility of developing specialized educational programs with FIDE’s participation. Special attention was given to the training of specialists in sports management. The possibility of creating a separate educational program tailored to the needs of the international chess community was also considered. The parties expressed interest in continuing the dialogue to more thoroughly develop potential areas of cooperation. Prospects for the development of chess in the Paralympic movement were discussed at a meeting with the President of the Hungarian Paralympic Committee, László Szabó. The meeting participants considered possible steps to further promote chess in Paralympic sports, including the use of European sporting events as a platform for developing this area. Issues of cooperation in the field of school chess were one of the topics of Timur Turlov’s meeting with the Hungarian Minister of Internal Affairs, Gábor Pósfai. The FIDE President emphasized the federation’s interest in expanding educational opportunities and developing chess programs for schoolchildren. Special attention was also given to engagement with the organizers of international chess competitions. Timur Turlov met with the founder of Norway Chess and the Total Chess World Championship Tour, Kjell Madland; the Chairman of the Board of Directors of Total Chess, Roy-André Tollefsen; and sports and media industry representative Rune Hauge. The parties exchanged views on the prospects for the development of international chess projects and possible formats of cooperation. The discussions were preliminary in nature and aimed at exploring potential opportunities for collaboration. Additionally, while in Budapest, Timur Turlov met with the Ambassador of the Republic of Kazakhstan to Hungary, Anel Bakytbekkyzy. Furthermore, the FIDE President held meetings with representatives of the national chess federations of several European countries.

title: Total Chess: Top scorers obtain 4/6 points on first day of group stage
summary:
The group stage of the Total Chess Pilot began in Budapest on Wednesday, with players contesting two games at a 45+30 time control. Six players finished the day with 4 points out of a possible 6: Fabiano Caruana, Alireza Firouzja (pictured), Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Ian Nepomniachtchi, Jan-Krzysztof Duda and Le Quang Liem. The football-style scoring system made an immediate difference, as Magnus Carlsen and Anish Giri - who drew both their encounters - find themselves trailing players who collected a win and a loss. | Photo: Michal Walusza / Total Chess

Two classical games in a single day

Following Tuesday's blitz tournament, the main event of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot began in Budapest on Wednesday. The 24 participants were divided into four groups of six, playing a double round-robin at the innovative (for elite tournaments) "fast classic" time control of 45 minutes plus 30-second increments per move.

Notably, this is the first time FIDE has applied such a time control to an elite tournament with games counting towards the official classical ratings. With two rounds scheduled each day, some of the strongest players in the world are playing two rated classical games on the same day (a rare if not unheard of occurrence in the history of the game). On Wednesday, each participant faced the same opponent twice, once with each colour.

Another distinctive feature is the use of football-style scoring: 3 points for a win, 1 for a draw and none for a loss. The effect was already apparent in Group C, where Magnus Carlsen and Anish Giri drew both their games to finish on 2 points each, behind Ian Nepomniachtchi, who collected a win and a draw for 4 points, and also behind Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and Haik Martirosyan, who exchanged victories with the black pieces to score 3 points each. Under this scoring system, a win and a loss are worth more than two draws.

No player managed to start the group stage with back-to-back wins on Wednesday. The top six scorers finished the day with 4 points out of a possible 6: Jan-Krzysztof Duda and Alireza Firouzja in Group A, Fabiano Caruana and Le Quang Liem in Group B, Ian Nepomniachtchi in Group C and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in Group D.

The event is taking place at the beautiful Anantara New York Palace Hotel in Budapest - thus, it is only natural that Hungarian legend Peter Leko played the first move for Hungary's number one Richard Rapport in the first round | Photo: Michal Walusza

Ian Nepomniachtchi scored a win (with white) and a draw against Abhimanyu Mishra to take the lead in Group C | Photo: Michal Walusza

Bibisara Assaubayeva struggled in the blitz event on Tuesday, but remarkably twice held draws against Wesley So in the fast classic games | Photo: Michal Walusza

Anish Giri and Magnus Carlsen, who have been members of the elite for nearly two decades now, played two fighting games which ended in draws | Photo: Michal Walusza

title: CBM 233: Aronian and Pragg shine
summary:
ChessBase Magazine offers a window to the world of professional chess.  Nagesh Havanur takes a look at the recent issue, CBM 233.  A total of 2911 games from the Biel and Norway tournaments (18 annotated), 10 opening surveys, 3 opening videos, demo lectures and several exercises for training. Annotators include Lubomir Ftacnik. Aydin Suleymanli and Le Quang Liem, among others. The icing on the cake is Anish Giri's analysis of two decisive games from the Quantbox Chennai Grandmasters Tournament. | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Deep and detailed annotations

There are tournaments and tournaments, and the annual Biel chess competition is more than a tournament. It's a festival open to one and all, be it a chess professional or an amateur. The event has an edition for every level of player, suitable for his or her standard.

The triathlon, though, is for stronger players, and this year it was won Levon Aronian (featured on the cover of this issue).

Tournament reports often focus on the success of the winner, so the performance of others close behind him is overlooked. In this issue, however, they receive a lot of recognition. Young Aydin Suleymanli came second and here he analyses his game with Le Quang Liem.

Le Quang Liem had won this Biel Chess Festival Tournament for three consecutive years before. This time he shared the third place with Yagiz Erdogmus. He did not do too badly. Here is a game analysed by the winner himself.

That still leaves open the question, "How did Aronian win this tournament?" At the Prize Distribution Ceremony he admitted laughingly, "I did not dream of winning against these young monsters". The genial grandmaster, now in mid-forties has a sunny temperament and, unlike more ambitious players, does not try to win every tournament. This sober, pragmatic approach earned him dividends in the Biel Competition. He was relaxed, and he took his chances when he saw them over the board. On occasion, he took crazy risks and managed to win even from lost positions. The following game is a fine example:

As in the game with Suleymanli that we saw, Aronian experimented in the opening so that his opponent would be on his own. A case in point is a rare line in the French Defence that he tried against Bluebaum. I think Black could try a principled continuation against this line:

Video: Biel Chess Festival

The battle of Norway

The brief report on Norway 2026 focuses on Magnus Carlsen's poor form rather than the incredible performance of Praggnanandhaa Rameshbaby who scored win after win after six rounds and two consecutive losses. Magnus lost to three opponents: Alireza Firouzja, Wesley So and Praggnanandhaa. Here is one of them analysed by Anish Giri:

In fairness to Magnus he did not do as badly as shown in the tournament table. Here is his win over the same opponent:

However, it was Pragg's performance that proved decisive in the end. Magnus himself was generous in his opinion of the young player:

I am a fan. I love watching him. He plays in a very aggressive way. He manages to put pressure on basically everybody, including myself.

(Interview, The Hindu , 11 September 2026)

Video: Norway Chess

Opening surveys

There are as many as ten articles on the openings ranging from the Sicilian to the Slav. Among others, two deserve special attention. The first is the analysis of the Alekhine-Chatard Attack (C13-C14) by Sergey Grigoriants. At first sight it appears that there is no easy way to meet White's offensive. However, Black can try a sideline that may solve his problems:

The second is a deep analysis of the Marshall Gambit against the Semi-Slav (D31) by Bàlazs Csonka. Here we have only room for an important encounter from the Candidates Tournament early this year:

Opening videos

There are three opening videos in this issue. The first of them is on the Saemisch Variation of the Nimzo-Indian (E24) by Ivan Sokolov. The second is on the English Defence (A40) by Danny King. The third is on the Exchange Variation of the Grünfeld (D85) by Mihail Marin.

Take your pick.

Besides opening surveys, this issue has standard features on tactics, strategy and the endgame.

Endgame play

In the regular column "Fundamental Endgame Knowledge", Karsten Müller offers a video lecture on the queen versus two minor pieces setup.

In his series on the fortress theme, Dorian Rogozenco offers a video lecture on opposite-coloured bishops with one side having two pawns.

This section also offers a column, "Readers write", in which we find contributions on the endgame by Zoran Petronijevic, Chris Edwards, Ingo Althoefer and Markus Hochgraefe.

Summing up

The main database of the issue has 2911 games, of which 18 are deeply annotated. There is much else in this DVD that deserves to be explored. Among the commentators I would like to make a special mention of Alvar Alonso Rosell. His annotations are deep and detailed, full of insight. It may be noted that there are more annotated games in the opening and training sections of this issue. Well, practice makes perfect.
